safety_verdicts.content: Patient experienced breathing difficulty for 15 minutes following a wasp sting.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated facts note the wasp sting timing and chest tightness/respiratory symptoms, but do not explicitly state breathing difficulty for 15 minutes following the sting.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Not documenting that breathing difficulty has persisted for ~15 minutes after the wasp sting reduces clarity about symptom duration and progression, which can affect risk stratification for evolving anaphylaxis. However, respiratory symptoms/chest tightness and the temporal link to the sting are still captured, so the immediate clinical response would likely be similar.

safety_verdicts.content: Patient denies any sensation of throat closing.
safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Gold states the patient denies throat closing sensation; generated facts do not document a denial of throat closing.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Failure to document a denial of throat-closing sensation can make the presentation appear more consistent with upper-airway involvement and may bias clinicians toward higher severity labeling of an allergic reaction. In this case, the patient is already being directed to emergency care due to breathing symptoms, so the incremental harm is limited.

safety_verdicts.eval_reasoning: Generated facts contain no allergy information; penicillin allergy is absent.
safety_verdicts.clinical_rationale: Omitting a penicillin allergy is clinically important because it can lead to inadvertent prescribing of a contraindicated antibiotic in subsequent care, potentially causing a serious allergic reaction. Even if not immediately relevant to the wasp-sting encounter, allergy documentation is a high-impact safety item across transitions of care.
